newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus - Bundesbank officials say EMU fears overdone.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Bundesbank officials say EMU fears overdone.

text.p: Two Bundesbank council members said on Tuesday that they believed fears of market tension in the run-up to European monetary union could be exaggerated, but one warned that the German mark could come under pressure.

Olaf Sievert, president of the regional central bank in the east German city of Leipzig, said that although he expected the two years before the euro's launch in 1999 to be difficult, extreme currency market tension was not likely to be a problem.

Looking ahead to possible problems, Sievert said, "I am not thinking here so much of the widespread fear that speculative trends on financial markets could create turbulence which will make the task of monetary policy more difficult."
Growing consensus in financial markets that EMU would start on time in 1999 meant that any speculation was more likely to be "stabilising speculation, and not destabilising speculation".
"There are possibly exaggerated worries here," he added.

His view was backed by fellow Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse, head of the regional central bank based in Hamburg, who said that "the current expectations...do not point to notable fluctations".
But Hesse warned that the German mark could see some weakness in the run-up to the 1999 start of EMU, as some investors might switch holdings into other currencies.
This possibility arose particularly because around 30 to 40 percent of marks in circulation were held abroad.

"No one can predict whether these mark holdings will be held until the start of monetary union and then exchanged into euros or will be exchanged earlier into other currencies," Hesse said. "Mark weakness for this reason cannot be ruled out with absolute certainty."
The officials were speaking at New Year receptions at their central banks. Their speeches were released in advance.

Both council members lashed out in their speeches at a proposal from France to set up a council which would form a political counterweight to the future European Central Bank, dealing primarily with exchange rate issues.

Sievert questioned the value of such a council given that its would have no decision-making power, even if its views did conflict with the ECB's commitment to price stability cemented in the Maastricht Treaty.
Hesse said the proposal showed that France, which has a tradition of state leadership in many areas, was still not fully committed to ceding powers to a supranational authority.
Turning to domestic issues, Sievert said the Bundesbank would have no grounds to raise interest rates any time soon and might even have scope to lower them further this economic cycle.
"I see nothing which could give us grounds to take a firmer grip on the monetary reins," he said.

It was hard to say whether there could be scope for further cuts in leading interest rates this cycle. The Bundesbank has held its Lombard and discount rates steady since April but it reduced a key money market rate in August.

Sievert said the outlook for German inflation continued to be favourable despite increases in raw materials prices. "The prospects for the future also look good," he said, noting annual German inflation was now running at around 1.4 percent.

This fact, together with expectations that money supply growth will slow in 1997, meant the Bundesbank did not have to be too concerned about its main policy indicator, M3 money supply, having overshot its growth target in 1996, he said.
Both officials expressed some concern that investment was not picking up as fast as had been hoped, which would give the economic upturn increased strength.
But they welcomed moderate wage deals as laying a good basis for continued inflation-free growth.
